name: Postcolonialism
summary: Postcolonialism studies and opposes the lasting political, economic and cultural legacy of European colonialism. Its theorists (Said, Spivak, Bhabha) argue that knowledge of colonised peoples was bound up with domination, that European claims of superiority and the category of the Other were constructed, and that independence did not end colonial structures. They disagree among themselves on Marxism versus poststructuralism.

scope: Postcolonial theory as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, a Yale open course and Roy's critical introduction define it: the humanities strand of Said (Orientalism), Spivak, Bhabha and Chakrabarty, concerned with knowledge and power, representation, the Other, hybridity and Eurocentrism. It leaves out the decolonization and neocolonialism strand (Fanon on violence, Nkrumah on economic dependence), which the Stanford Encyclopedia treats as a separate body of theory, and the settler-colonial critiques of postcolonialism.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Said's foundational argument, as the Stanford Encyclopedia, the Yale lecture and Roy report it, is that knowledge of the colonised is bound up with power, so the assumption of value-free scholarship is rejected.

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Roy presents postcolonial theory as exposing the European claim of inherent superiority over the barbaric Other, including the mission civilisatrice, as an ideology of domination, and the Stanford Encyclopedia reports the anticolonial rejection of the civilizing claim.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Roy and the Stanford Encyclopedia present colonialism as ideological, racial and economic domination of the colonised, which postcolonial theory sets out to oppose.

race-social-construct.rationale: Roy states that Fanon, Said, Spivak and Bhabha argue that race is a social construct, produced by defining the European norm through the creation of the Other.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Roy presents the unalterability of colonial frontiers (uti possidetis) as a Western construct that, from a postcolonial perspective, forced peoples to join or fragment.

notes: Themes searched: economy, world, means, government, culture and law, in the Stanford Encyclopedia, Roy and the Yale lecture; the Indigenous-law material in Roy is the author's application, not a tenet. The record is split between anticolonial and poststructuralist strands, so most statements are null. Said and Spivak could not be obtained from an acceptable open copy, so only scholarly accounts of them are cited. Fanon's own text was set aside because the catalog treats him as a defining author of decolonization.
